patient.name: Kwame Asante
patient.complaint: Fever, dry cough and worsening breathlessness for 8 days; cannot smell his food
background: His granddaughter tested positive for Covid-19 last week

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with fever, dry cough, anosmia, hypoxia, lymphopenia and bilateral infiltrates, often with a contact history; or complication questions (ARDS, PE).

points: Kwame, 67: fever and **dry cough** for 8 days.
Now breathless walking to the bathroom.

steps.lead: His granddaughter's positive test points to **SARS-CoV-2**, caught by droplets and aerosols at a family meal.
Kwame's **age and obesity** put him at risk of severe disease; immunosuppression or HIV would add more.
Fever, dry cough, myalgia, breathlessness and **anosmia** with hypoxia and tachypnoea: viral pneumonia, the severe end.

steps.q: Which single feature most points to Covid-19 over other viral illnesses?
steps.r: Fever, cough and myalgia occur in flu too. **Anosmia** is the distinctive Covid-19 clue.

steps.title: Covid-19 vs influenza vs bacterial pneumonia
head: Feature
Covid-19
Influenza
Bacterial pneumonia

steps.lead: Kwame's falling sats make **ARDS** the main fear; immobility and inflammation also raise his **PE** risk.

steps.text: Do not assume a normal-feeling patient is fine: Covid-19 can cause **silent hypoxia**. Always check the saturation.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?' (PCR) and 'most likely finding' questions on bloods (raised CRP, lymphopenia) and imaging (bilateral infiltrates).

steps.r: **PCR** is the gold standard. Lateral flow is quicker but less sensitive; antibodies show past infection.

steps.lead: Kwame's nose and throat swab goes for **SARS-CoV-2 PCR**; it returns positive within hours.

steps.title: Admission bloods
steps.text: A normal total white count with **lymphopenia** and raised CRP is the classic Covid pattern.

steps.lead: Kwame's **CRP 98** and **lymphocytes 0.6** fit; a raised D-dimer is common in Covid and does not itself mean PE.

visual.title: Chest X-ray on admission
visual.caption: **Bilateral** patchy peripheral infiltrates, mid and lower zones: typical of COVID-19 pneumonitis, unlike one lobe in bacterial pneumonia.

steps.lead: Kwame's film shows **bilateral infiltrates**; CT would show ground-glass change if the X-ray was unclear.

steps.text: A negative **lateral flow** test does not exclude Covid-19 in a typical admission. Send a **PCR**.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate management?' with severity as the decider: supportive for mild, dexamethasone plus remdesivir if on oxygen, tocilizumab if ventilated, early antivirals for high-risk outpatients.

visual.title: Oxygen saturation on air
visual.label: Kwame 89%
visual.caption: Kwame needs **supplemental oxygen**: that is the trigger for dexamethasone and remdesivir.

steps.q: Kwame needs 4 L/min oxygen to keep sats above 94%. What do you add?
steps.r: Needing **supplemental oxygen** triggers dexamethasone 6 mg daily with remdesivir. Tocilizumab is for those needing ventilation.

steps.lead: Kwame starts **dexamethasone 6 mg daily** with **remdesivir** because he needs oxygen.
Kwame is **admitted** for oxygen and gets **LMWH** prophylaxis; if he needed ventilation, **tocilizumab** would be added.

steps.title: Covid-19 treatment ladder
nodes: Mild: paracetamol and fluids at home
High-risk outpatient: Paxlovid and/or remdesivir early
steps.caption: Each step is triggered by severity.

steps.lead: His granddaughter, with mild disease, needs only **paracetamol and fluids**.
Had Kwame been **HIV-positive** with mild early disease, he would get **Paxlovid** or remdesivir early to prevent progression.

visual.title: Kwame's response to treatment
visual.caption: Dexamethasone dampens the inflammatory response: CRP and oxygen need fall together.

steps.lead: Kwame's care follows the **NHS/NICE Covid-19 rapid guideline** for suspected or confirmed pneumonia.

steps.text: Dexamethasone is **not** for mild disease without oxygen need. It helps only once the patient is hypoxic.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: the receptor (ACE2), why severe disease is inflammatory (hence steroids and tocilizumab), why anticoagulate, and how the antivirals work.

steps.lead: The virus's **spike protein** latched onto **ACE2** on Kwame's airway cells, which is why it targets the respiratory tract.

steps.title: From infection to ARDS
steps.caption: Late severe disease is driven by the host, not the virus.

steps.lead: Kwame's lungs are damaged mostly by his **own inflammatory response**, so **dexamethasone** helps.

steps.q: Why does tocilizumab help in severe Covid-19?
steps.r: Tocilizumab is an **anti-IL-6 receptor** antibody that damps the cytokine storm. Remdesivir hits viral RNA polymerase.

steps.lead: Endothelial injury and inflammation make Kwame **hypercoagulable**, so he gets LMWH to prevent VTE.
**Nirmatrelvir** blocks the viral protease; **ritonavir** slows its metabolism to boost levels. Remdesivir stops viral RNA replication.

steps.text: Antivirals work **early** (viral phase); steroids and tocilizumab work **late** (inflammatory phase).

mcq.q: Which symptom is most distinctive of Covid-19?
mcq.r: **Loss of smell** is the distinctive feature.

mcq.q: Which group is at particularly high risk of severe complications?
What is the major complication of severe Covid-19 pneumonia?
What is given to patients needing supplemental oxygen?
Which drug is used for patients requiring ventilation?
Which receptor does SARS-CoV-2 use to enter cells?

technique.stem: A 54 year old woman has had fever, dry cough and muscle aches for 6 days. For 3 days she has been unable to smell or taste her food. Her husband had similar symptoms last week. Her temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 128/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. There are fine bibasal crackles.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Dry cough, fever, myalgia, **anosmia**, contact, hypoxia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Usually productive cough, rigors and focal signs; anosmia is not a feature.
Abrupt onset with myalgia, but anosmia points to Covid-19.
Linked to water systems, with hyponatraemia and diarrhoea.
Needs immunosuppression (e.g. HIV with low CD4).

steps.x: **A. Covid-19.** Rule: fever + dry cough + **anosmia** + contact = Covid-19.

technique.stem: A 61 year old man has fever, dry cough and loss of smell for 5 days. His temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 132/84 mmHg and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. A lateral flow test at home was negative.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
o: SARS-CoV-2 PCR on a nasopharyngeal swab

clues: lateral flow test at home was negative
steps.x: Typical Covid; negative lateral flow does not exclude.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Supports but does not confirm the diagnosis.
Less sensitive; PCR is the gold standard.
Shows past infection or vaccination.
For bacteria, not SARS-CoV-2.

steps.x: **C. SARS-CoV-2 PCR on a nasopharyngeal swab.** Rule: gold standard = **PCR** for SARS-CoV-2.

technique.stem: A 38 year old man with HIV has had a sore throat, dry cough and fever for 2 days. A PCR test is positive for SARS-CoV-2. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 88 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. His chest is clear.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate management?

steps.x: Mild early disease in a **high-risk** patient.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Only if needing oxygen; his sats are 98%.
An influenza drug.
Right for low-risk mild disease, but he is **HIV-positive** (high risk).
Only if ventilated.

steps.x: **B. Nirmatrelvir with ritonavir.** Rule: high-risk + mild early = **Paxlovid** and/or remdesivir.

technique.stem: A 70 year old woman with Covid-19 is prescribed nirmatrelvir with ritonavir. A pharmacist explains that ritonavir has little direct antiviral effect at this dose.
technique.q: Which is the most likely reason ritonavir is included?
o: It binds ACE2 to block viral entry
It inhibits the metabolism of nirmatrelvir
It reduces cytokine production as a steroid

steps.x: A drug mechanism question about the booster.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: It boosts nirmatrelvir levels by inhibiting its metabolism.

elim: No drug here blocks ACE2.
That is tocilizumab.
That is remdesivir.
That is dexamethasone.

steps.x: **C. It inhibits the metabolism of nirmatrelvir.** Rule: nirmatrelvir = protease inhibitor; ritonavir = **booster**.

practice.stem: A 59 year old man has had fever, dry cough and fatigue for 7 days and has lost his sense of smell. His temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 102 bpm, BP 134/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Fever, dry cough, anosmia and hypoxia with lymphopenia and raised CRP is Covid-19; bacterial pneumonia gives a neutrophilia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: No hypoxia or systemic illness in bronchitis.
No anosmia in flu; anosmia and lymphopenia favour Covid-19.
Neutrophilia and lobar consolidation would be expected.
No fever, anosmia or bilateral infiltrates.

steps.x: **B. Covid-19.** Rule: anosmia + lymphopenia + hypoxia = Covid-19.

practice.stem: A 64 year old woman with confirmed Covid-19 has been unwell for 6 days with fever and dry cough. Her temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on her full blood count?
practice.e: Lymphopenia with a raised CRP is typical of Covid-19; neutrophilia points to bacterial infection.

steps.x: A 'most likely finding' question: recall the classic blood result.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Seen in allergy, parasites, some drugs.
Seen in myeloproliferative disease, not Covid.
Chronic hypoxia or primary disease, not acute infection.
A very high neutrophil count suggests bacterial sepsis.

steps.x: **E. Lymphopenia.** Rule: Covid-19 bloods = **lymphopenia and raised CRP**.

practice.stem: A 72 year old man has had fever, dry cough and breathlessness for 9 days after his wife had Covid-19. His temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 130/76 mmHg and oxygen saturation 90% breathing air. His chest X-ray is shown (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Bilateral peripheral mid and lower zone infiltrates.

practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Bilateral infiltrates in a hypoxic febrile contact of a Covid-19 case is Covid-19 pneumonia; pneumococcus gives lobar consolidation.

steps.x: Image-based diagnosis: read the CXR in context.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: No orthopnoea or oedema; fever and contact favour infection.
Gives single-lobe consolidation, not bilateral peripheral changes.
Chronic, not a 9-day febrile illness.
Upper zone cavitation over weeks, with weight loss.

steps.x: **A. Covid-19 pneumonia.** Rule: bilateral infiltrates + contact + hypoxia = Covid-19 pneumonia.

practice.stem: A 66 year old woman is in intensive care on day 10 of Covid-19. Despite high-flow oxygen her saturation has fallen to 84%. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm, BP 104/66 mmHg and respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute. Chest X-ray shows dense bilateral opacities. Echocardiogram shows normal left ventricular function.
practice.q: Which is the most likely complication?
practice.e: Refractory hypoxia with bilateral opacities and normal LV function in severe Covid-19 is ARDS.

steps.x: Complication question: severe hypoxia with bilateral opacities.
Bilateral opacities, refractory hypoxia, not cardiac.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Gives a localised collection, not bilateral white-out.
LV function is normal.
Unilateral, with absent breath sounds.
Does not cause dense bilateral opacities.

steps.x: **A. Acute respiratory distress syndrome.** Rule: severe Covid + bilateral opacities + normal heart = **ARDS**.

practice.stem: A 58 year old man admitted with Covid-19 pneumonia 5 days ago suddenly develops pleuritic left-sided chest pain and worsening breathlessness. His pulse rate is 124 bpm, BP 112/70 mmHg and oxygen saturation 88% on 2 L/min oxygen. His left calf is swollen.
practice.q: Which is the most likely complication?
practice.e: Sudden pleuritic pain, hypoxia, tachycardia and a swollen calf in hospitalised Covid-19 is PE, from the hypercoagulable state.

steps.x: Complication: sudden deterioration in a hospitalised Covid patient.
Sudden pleuritic pain, tachycardia, hypoxia, swollen calf.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Develops gradually, without pleuritic pain or calf swelling.
Chest pain with troponin rise and arrhythmias, not calf swelling.
No calf swelling; reduced breath sounds.
Gradual, with purulent sputum and fever.

steps.x: **D. Pulmonary embolism.** Rule: Covid is **hypercoagulable**: sudden pleuritic pain + calf swelling = PE.

practice.stem: A 29 year old man has Covid-19 with fever and cough. He is HIV-positive, has not been taking antiretroviral therapy and his CD4 count is low. He also has hay fever, well-controlled asthma and a penicillin allergy. His temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 120/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which feature most increases his risk of severe complications?
practice.e: HIV-positive status, especially untreated with a low CD4 count, confers a high risk of severe Covid-19 complications.

steps.x: Risk factor question: pick the strongest one in the stem.
Untreated HIV with low CD4 = immunosuppression.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Not a risk factor for severe disease.
A weak factor compared with immunosuppression.
Irrelevant to Covid severity.
Well-controlled asthma is a weak factor compared with untreated HIV.

steps.x: **C. HIV infection.** Rule: **HIV-positive** status confers high risk of severe Covid-19.

practice.stem: A 47 year old woman has had fever, dry cough and anosmia for 4 days. Her temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 92 bpm, BP 126/78 mmHg and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
practice.e: PCR for SARS-CoV-2 is the gold-standard diagnostic test.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Supports severity assessment; does not confirm.
For PE.
Shows past exposure.
For bacterial pneumonia.

practice.stem: A 69 year old man with PCR-confirmed Covid-19 is admitted with worsening breathlessness. His temperature is 38.5°C, pulse rate 106 bpm, BP 128/74 mmHg and oxygen saturation 90% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on chest X-ray?
o: Single lobar consolidation with air bronchograms
practice.e: Covid-19 pneumonia typically shows bilateral, often peripheral, infiltrates; lobar consolidation suggests bacterial pneumonia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Sarcoidosis.
TB or Staph. aureus or Klebsiella.
Bacterial pneumonia.
Malignancy, empyema or heart failure.

steps.x: **B. Bilateral peripheral infiltrates.** Rule: Covid CXR/CT = **bilateral infiltrates**.

practice.stem: A 34 year old woman has had fever, dry cough and anosmia for 3 days. PCR is positive for SARS-CoV-2. She has no medical history. Her temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 84 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Paracetamol and oral fluids at home
practice.e: Mild Covid-19 in a low-risk patient needs supportive care only; dexamethasone helps only those needing oxygen.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: She is low risk and not hypoxic.
Only if needing oxygen.
No bacterial infection.
Only if ventilated.

steps.x: **D. Paracetamol and oral fluids at home.** Rule: mild Covid = **paracetamol and hydration**.

practice.stem: A 71 year old man with Covid-19 pneumonia needs 4 L/min oxygen to keep his saturation above 94%. His temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 100 bpm and BP 136/80 mmHg. He is not ventilated.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
practice.e: Patients needing supplemental oxygen get dexamethasone 6 mg daily with remdesivir; tocilizumab is added if ventilation is required.

steps.x: Management: oxygen need is the trigger.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Ineffective; not recommended.
For influenza.
Insufficient: he needs oxygen.
Ventilated patients; and not alone.

steps.x: **A. Dexamethasone 6 mg daily and remdesivir.** Rule: on oxygen = **dexamethasone 6 mg + remdesivir**.

practice.stem: A 63 year old woman with severe Covid-19 is intubated and ventilated in intensive care. She is already receiving dexamethasone and prophylactic LMWH. Her pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP 108/64 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate additional treatment?
practice.e: Patients requiring ventilation get tocilizumab; Paxlovid is for early mild disease in high-risk patients.

steps.x: Management: escalate for the most severe disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: No benefit in viral Covid-19.
Not effective.
Influenza only.
For mild early disease in high-risk outpatients.

practice.stem: A 45 year old man has Covid-19 with anosmia and a dry cough. A student asks how the virus enters his respiratory epithelial cells.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
practice.e: SARS-CoV-2 enters via its spike protein binding ACE2 on respiratory epithelium; haemagglutinin–sialic acid binding is influenza.

steps.x: Mechanism: match the virus to its receptor.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: HIV entry.
Influenza entry.
Influenza release, not entry.
Cholera-type toxins.

steps.x: **D. Spike protein binding to ACE2.** Rule: SARS-CoV-2 = **spike + ACE2**; influenza = haemagglutinin + sialic acid.

glossary.Covid-19: Illness caused by the SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus, ranging from a cold to severe pneumonia.
glossary.aerosols: Tiny airborne particles that can carry virus over longer distances than droplets.
glossary.anosmia: Loss of the sense of smell; a distinctive Covid-19 symptom.
glossary.hypoxia: Low oxygen levels in the blood or tissues.
glossary.silent hypoxia: Low oxygen saturation in a patient who does not feel very breathless.
glossary.ARDS: Acute respiratory distress syndrome: inflammatory lung injury with bilateral opacities and severe hypoxia, not due to heart failure.
glossary.lymphopenia: A low lymphocyte count; typical in Covid-19.
glossary.CRP: C-reactive protein; a blood marker of inflammation.
glossary.D-dimer: Fibrin breakdown product; raised in clotting and often in Covid-19.
glossary.PCR: Polymerase chain reaction: detects viral genetic material; gold standard for Covid-19.
glossary.lateral flow: Rapid antigen test; quick but less sensitive than PCR.
glossary.bilateral infiltrates: Shadowing in both lungs on imaging, typical of Covid-19 pneumonia.
glossary.ground-glass: Hazy CT lung change through which vessels are still seen.
glossary.dexamethasone: Corticosteroid given at 6 mg daily to Covid-19 patients needing oxygen.
glossary.remdesivir: IV antiviral that inhibits viral RNA replication.
glossary.tocilizumab: Antibody against the IL-6 receptor, used in ventilated Covid-19 patients.
glossary.IL-6: Interleukin-6, an inflammatory cytokine central to the cytokine storm.
glossary.Paxlovid: Oral nirmatrelvir plus ritonavir for early Covid-19 in high-risk patients.
glossary.nirmatrelvir: Antiviral that inhibits the SARS-CoV-2 main protease.
glossary.ritonavir: Booster that inhibits nirmatrelvir's metabolism (CYP3A4) to raise its levels.
glossary.protease: Viral enzyme that cuts long proteins into working parts; blocked by nirmatrelvir.
glossary.ACE2: Angiotensin-converting enzyme 2: the cell receptor SARS-CoV-2 uses to enter.
glossary.spike protein: Surface protein of SARS-CoV-2 that binds ACE2.
glossary.tropism: The preference of a virus for particular cells or tissues.
glossary.cytokine storm: An excessive inflammatory response that damages the body's own tissues.
glossary.hypercoagulable: More prone than normal to forming blood clots.
glossary.VTE: Venous thromboembolism: DVT or pulmonary embolism.
glossary.LMWH: Low molecular weight heparin, e.g. enoxaparin; injectable anticoagulant.
glossary.PE: Pulmonary embolism: a clot blocking a lung artery.
glossary.HIV: Human immunodeficiency virus, which weakens the immune system.
glossary.multi-organ failure: Failure of two or more organ systems in severe illness.
